claim: Drosophila Malpighian tubules are two pairs of tubules that converge through common ureters onto the midgut-hindgut junction.
source: Drosophila excretory system, so-called Malpighian tubules, are two pairs of tubules converge through common ureters onto midgut-hindgut junction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Denholm and Skaer, 2009; Dow, 2009; Singh et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Denholm and Skaer, 2009; Dow, 2009; Singh et al., 2007) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Each pair of renal tubules can be mainly divided into three segments: ureter, lower tubule and upper tubule.
source: Each pair of renal tubules can be mainly divided into three segments: ureter, lower tubule and upper tubule (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) (Singh et al., 2007; Sözen et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations (Singh et al., 2007; Sözen et al., 1997) and references to figures showing the anatomical structure.

claim: The ureter can be further divided into lower and upper regions.
source: The ureter can be further divided into lower and upper regions (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1B showing the anatomical divisions.

claim: Renal stem cells (RSCs) are dispersed in the adult ureter and lower tubule regions.
source: Renal stem cells (RSCs) were found to be dispersed in the adult ureter and lower tubule regions (Figure 1B) (Singh et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2007 and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: RSCs are not found in larval renal tubules.
source: Renal stem cells (RSCs) were found to be dispersed in the adult ureter and lower tubule regions (Figure 1B) (Singh et al., 2007) but not in the larval renal tubules
evidence: The claim is stated explicitly in the text and supported by citation.

claim: Adult RSCs are likely derived from progenitors within the midgut region.
source: Earlier work (Takashima et al., 2013) and our independent observations found that adult RSCs are likely to be derived from progenitors within the midgut region.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takashima et al., 2013 and the authors' own observations.

claim: Midgut progenitors and renal progenitors both express Escargot (Esg).
source: Midgut progenitors (MPs) and renal progenitors (RPs), although both express Snail-type transcription factor Escargot (Esg), are distinct populations of precursor cells in terms of lineage composition and functionality
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated in the text describing the characteristics of these cell populations.

claim: Midgut progenitors/stem cells undergo asymmetric cell divisions to self-renew and differentiate into enteroendocrine (EE) cells and enterocytes (ECs).
source: midgut progenitors/stem cells undergo asymmetric cell divisions to self-renew and meanwhile differentiate into hormone/peptide-secreting enteroendocrine (EE) cells and nutrient-absorbing enterocytes (ECs) (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006 and Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006.

claim: Renal progenitors undergo asymmetric, self-renewing divisions to give rise to principal cells that mediate organic cation and solute transport.
source: in contrast, renal progenitors undergo asymmetric, self-renewing divisions to give rise to principal cells that mediate organic cation and solute transport (Singh et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Singh et al., 2007.

claim: During metamorphosis, a small subset of Esg+ progenitors migrate away from the midgut and onto the renal tubules.
source: Intriguingly, we observed that, during metamorphosis, a small subset of Esg+ progenitors appeared to migrate away from the midgut and onto the renal tubules (Figure 1C–E)
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' observations and reference to Figure 1C-E showing the migration.

claim: Migrating Esg+ progenitors terminally differentiate into new Cut+ principal cells.
source: where they terminally differentiated into new Cut+principal cells (arrowheads in Figure 1D), replacing the old Cut- principal cells in the lower ureter region (arrowheads in Figure 1C) (Takashima et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C-D and citation to Takashima et al., 2013.

claim: Old Cut- principal cells in the lower ureter region are replaced by new Cut+ principal cells during metamorphosis.
source: where they terminally differentiated into new Cut+principal cells (arrowheads in Figure 1D), replacing the old Cut- principal cells in the lower ureter region (arrowheads in Figure 1C) (Takashima et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C-D and citation to Takashima et al., 2013.

claim: Cut is expressed in adult renal stem cells but not intestinal stem cells.
source: Cut is expressed in adult renal stem cells (arrowheads in F, F') but not intestinal stem cells (ISC; arrowheads in G, G').
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1F-G' showing differential Cut expression.

claim: Cut was originally identified as a binary identity switch between subtypes of neurons in the peripheral nervous systems (PNS) of Drosophila.
source: Cut was originally identified as a binary identity switch between subtypes of neurons in the peripheral nervous systems (PNS) of Drosophila (Bodmer et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bodmer et al., 1987.

claim: Cut is both necessary and sufficient in specifying neuronal identities in fly PNS.
source: Compelling evidence demonstrated that Cut is both necessary and sufficient in specifying neuronal identities in fly PNS (Blochlinger et al., 1991; Bodmer et al., 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blochlinger et al., 1991 and Bodmer et al., 1987.

claim: Cut was undetectable in any Esg+ progenitors in third instar larval (L3) midguts.
source: Cut was undetectable in any Esg+ progenitors in third instar larval (L3) midguts (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2A showing absence of Cut expression.

claim: At the onset of metamorphosis (0 hr APF), a few clusters of Esg+ progenitors in closest proximity to the midgut-hindgut boundary started to exhibit Cut expression.
source: At the onset of metamorphosis (0 hr after puparium formation (APF)), a few clusters of Esg+ progenitors in closest proximity to the midgut-hindgut boundary started to exhibit Cut expression (white arrowheads in Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2B showing Cut expression at 0 hr APF.

claim: At 0.5 hr APF, 20–30 Esg+ progenitors in 5–6 clusters specifically expressed Cut.
source: At 0.5 hr APF, 20–30 Esg+ progenitors in 5–6 clusters specifically expressed Cut (yellow bracket in Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: By 1 hr APF, midgut progenitor islands merged together and the Cut+ progenitors aligned along the midgut-hindgut border in 1–3 rows.
source: By 1 hr APF, midgut progenitor islands merged together and the Cut+ progenitors aligned along the midgut-hindgut border in 1–3 rows (yellow bracket in Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2D showing the alignment of Cut+ progenitors.

claim: Starting at 3 hr APF, Esg+ Cut+ progenitors migrated across the midgut border and entered the renal tubules.
source: Starting at 3 hr APF, Esg+ Cut+ progenitors migrated across the midgut border and entered the renal tubules (yellow bracket in Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2E showing migration at 3 hr APF.

claim: Cut- principal cells in the lower ureter region were engulfed and expelled into the pupal midgut.
source: Cut- principal cells in the lower ureter region were engulfed and expelled into the pupal midgut (pink arrowheads in Figure 2E) (González-Morales et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2E and citation to González-Morales et al., 2015.

claim: Cut+ progenitors occupied the lower ureter region and differentiated into Esg- Cut+ new principal cells.
source: Cut+ progenitors in turn occupied the lower ureter region (Figure 2F) and differentiated into Esg- Cut+ new principal cells (cyan arrowheads in Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to Figure 2F-G showing occupation and differentiation.

claim: At the onset of metamorphosis, Cut+ progenitors expressed midgut progenitor marker Delta (Dl).
source: At the onset of metamorphosis, Cut+ progenitors expressed midgut progenitor marker Delta (Dl) (arrowheads in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B showing Dl expression.

claim: By 9 hr APF, Cut+ progenitors along the renal tubules completely shut down Dl expression.
source: By 9 hr APF, Cut+ progenitors along the renal tubules completely shut down Dl expression (arrowheads in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1D showing absence of Dl expression.

claim: Cut is dispensable for progenitor mobility.
source: Upon cut knockdown by esg-Gal4, the migration of the small subset of Esg+ progenitors onto renal tubules remained relatively normal (Figure 3A–D'), indicating that Cut is dispensable for progenitor mobility.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing normal migration upon cut knockdown, referenced in Figure 3A-D'.

claim: In wild type renal tubules, Esg- lacZ+ cells derived from Esg+ lacZ+ RPs were found in the lower ureter region.
source: In wild type renal tubules, Esg- lacZ+ cells derived from Esg+ lacZ+ RPs (white arrowheads in Figure 3C,C') were found in the lower ureter region (brackets in Figure 3C,C').
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3C,C'.

claim: Esg- lacZ+ cells in wild type renal tubules were polyploid, new Cut+ principal cells.
source: These Esg- lacZ+ cells were polyploid, new Cut+ principal cells (white arrowheads in Figure 3C,C')
evidence: The claim is supported by characterization of cells shown in Figure 3C,C'.

claim: cut knockdown by esg-GAL4 caused the majority of flies to die at late pupal or early adult stages (90.3%, n = 567).
source: cut knockdown by esg-GAL4 caused the majority of flies to die at late pupal or early adult stages (90.3%, n = 567).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative survival data from the experiment.

claim: Adult escaper flies with cut knockdown lacked the whole lower ureter region.
source: The adult escaper flies lacked the whole lower ureter region (Figure 3D,D')
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic analysis shown in Figure 3D,D'.

claim: Upon cut depletion, Esg- lacZ+ cells derived from cut-RNAi RPs were dispersed throughout the ureter and lower tubule regions.
source: In contrast to the wild type control (Figure 3C,E), Esg- lacZ+ cells derived from cut-RNAi RPs were dispersed throughout the ureter and lower tubule regions (white arrowheads in Figure 3D').
evidence: The claim is supported by lineage tracing data shown in Figure 3D'.

claim: Upon cut depletion, Esg- lacZ+ cells derived from RPs were diploid, Cut- and expressed Prospero (Pros).
source: Strikingly, these Esg- lacZ+ cells were diploid, Cut- (Figure 3D,D'), and expressed Prospero (Pros) (Figure 3F,F'), a typical marker for EE cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by characterization of cells shown in Figure 3D,D' and 3F,F'.

claim: Upon cut depletion, Esg+ progenitors migrate normally onto the renal tubules, yet fail to switch into renal identity and differentiate into midgut cells along renal tubules.
source: These results strongly suggested that, upon cut depletion, Esg+ progenitors migrate normally onto the renal tubules, yet fail to switch into renal identity and differentiate into midgut cells along renal tubules.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing normal migration but altered differentiation.

claim: Wild type control MARCM clones residing in the midgut contain Pros+ EE cells.
source: Wild type control MARCM clones residing in the midgut but not ureter region (pink arrowheads in G and I) contain Pros+ EE cells (white arrowhead in G)
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM clonal analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Wild type control MARCM clones residing in the midgut contain Pdm1+ ECs.
source: Wild type control MARCM clones residing in the midgut but not ureter region (pink arrowheads in G and I) contain Pros+ EE cells (white arrowhead in G) and Pdm1+ ECs (white arrowhead in I).
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM clonal analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: cut mutant clones at ureter region contain Pros+ EEs.
source: In sharp contrast, cut mutant clones at ureter region contain Pros+ EEs (yellow arrowheads in H)
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM clonal analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: cut mutant clones at ureter region contain Pdm1+ ECs.
source: In sharp contrast, cut mutant clones at ureter region contain Pros+ EEs (yellow arrowheads in H) or Pdm1+ ECs (yellow arrowheads in J).
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM clonal analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: As a consequence of cut depletion from Esg+ progenitors, both the total length of the ureter region and the number of principal cells in ureter were sharply reduced.
source: Moreover, as a consequence of cut depletion from Esg+ progenitors, both the total length of the ureter region (Figure 3K) and the number of principal cells in ureter (Figure 3L) were sharply reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3K-L.

claim: Cut is necessary for MP-to-RP identity switch.
source: Taken together, our results clearly demonstrated that Cut is necessary for MP-to-RP identity switch.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing loss of renal identity upon cut depletion.

claim: In wild type MARCM clones derived from single MPs, GFP+ polyploid cells were Pdm1+ ECs.
source: In wild type MARCM clones derived from single MPs, GFP+ polyploid cells were Pdm1+ ECs (white arrowheads in Figure 3M).
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM clonal analysis shown in Figure 3M.

claim: MARCM clones derived from Cut-overexpressing MPs mainly contained Pdm1- Cut+ polyploid cells.
source: In contrast, MARCM clones derived from Cut-overexpressing MPs mainly contained Pdm1- Cut+ polyploid cells (yellow arrowheads in Figure 3M)
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM clonal analysis shown in Figure 3M.

claim: Cut-overexpressing MPs were converted into RPs that in turn differentiated into principal cells in midgut region.
source: MARCM clones derived from Cut-overexpressing MPs mainly contained Pdm1- Cut+ polyploid cells (yellow arrowheads in Figure 3M), strongly suggesting that MPs were converted into RPs that in turn differentiated into principal cells in midgut region.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the MARCM clonal analysis data showing ectopic principal cell formation.

claim: Cut acts as a master switch in dictating natural midgut-to-renal progenitor identity conversion.
source: Collectively, our observations reinforced the idea that Cut acts as a master switch in dictating natural midgut-to-renal progenitor identity conversion (Figure 3N).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence showing Cut is both necessary and sufficient for the identity switch.

claim: The Wnt/Wingless (Wg) ligand was expressed in a narrow zone of 2–3 rows of cells right at the midgut-hindgut boundary, starting from early larval stages.
source: After examining the distribution pattern of various signaling molecules or receptors at the onset of metamorphosis, we found that, in accordance with previous observations (Fox and Spradling, 2009; Takashima et al., 2008; Tian et al., 2016), the Wnt/Wingless (Wg) ligand (Clevers and Nusse, 2012; Loh et al., 2016) was expressed in a narrow zone of 2–3 rows of cells right at the midgut-hindgut boundary, starting from early larval stages (Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' observations, citations to previous work (Fox and Spradling, 2009; Takashima et al., 2008; Tian et al., 2016), and references to figures.

claim: At the onset of metamorphosis, 2–3 clusters of progenitors in closest proximity to the stripe of Wg-producing cells started to turn on Cut expression.
source: At the onset of metamorphosis, 2–3 clusters of progenitors in closest proximity to the stripe of Wg-producing cells started to turn on Cut expression (arrowheads in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Around 0.5 hr APF, Cut was expressed in 5–6 progenitor islands adjacent to the Wg-secreting cells.
source: Around 0.5 hr APF, Cut was expressed in 5–6 progenitor islands adjacent to the Wg-secreting cells (arrowheads in Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Some Cut+ progenitor islands were not in direct contact with the Wg-producing band, suggesting the existence of Wg morphogen gradient.
source: Some Cut+ progenitor islands were not in direct contact with the Wg-producing band (arrowheads in Figure 4D), suggesting the existence of Wg morphogen gradient.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the spatial distribution pattern observed in Figure 4D.

claim: At 1 hr APF, peripheral cells surrounding progenitor islands partially opened up, allowing Cut+ progenitor islands to merge with each other.
source: At 1 hr APF, peripheral cells surrounding progenitor islands (Mathur et al., 2010) partially opened up, allowing Cut+ progenitor islands to merge with each other (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4E and citation to Mathur et al., 2010.

claim: A clear boundary between Cut+ and Cut- progenitors could be delineated at 1 hr APF.
source: A clear boundary between Cut+ and Cut- progenitors could be delineated (dashed lines in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), suggesting the spatial precision of the inductive cue.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Wg signaling activity, as reflected by the Fz3-GFP reporter, was only detectable in a few rows of MPs proximal to Wg-secreting cells.
source: Wg signaling activity, as faithfully reflected by the Fz3-GFP reporter (Sivasankaran et al., 2000; Tian et al., 2016), was only detectable in a few rows of MPs proximal to Wg-secreting cells (closed arrowheads in Figure 4F)
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 4F and citations to Sivasankaran et al., 2000 and Tian et al., 2016.

claim: Specific knockdown of Wg within Wg-producing cells at midgut-hindgut boundary resulted in diminished Cut expression in Esg+ progenitors.
source: Indeed, specific knockdown of Wg within Wg-producing cells at midgut-hindgut boundary, by wg-Gal4 (Alexandre et al., 2014), resulted in diminished Cut expression in Esg+ progenitors (arrowheads in Figure 4G,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G,H and citation to Alexandre et al., 2014.

claim: Inhibition of Wg signaling through overexpression of ΔN-TCF in Esg+ progenitors completely abolished Cut induction.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of Wg signaling through overexpression of either a dominant-negative form of the Wnt pathway effector TCF (ΔN-TCF) (van de Wetering et al., 1997) or a constitutively-active form of the Wnt pathway inhibitor GSK3β/Shaggy (Sgg-CA) (Bourouis, 2002) in Esg+ progenitors completely abolished Cut induction (brackets in Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I and citations to van de Wetering et al., 1997 and Bourouis, 2002.

claim: Inhibition of Wg signaling through overexpression of Sgg-CA in Esg+ progenitors completely abolished Cut induction.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of Wg signaling through overexpression of either a dominant-negative form of the Wnt pathway effector TCF (ΔN-TCF) (van de Wetering et al., 1997) or a constitutively-active form of the Wnt pathway inhibitor GSK3β/Shaggy (Sgg-CA) (Bourouis, 2002) in Esg+ progenitors completely abolished Cut induction (brackets in Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4I and citations to van de Wetering et al., 1997 and Bourouis, 2002.

claim: Upon depletion of Disheveled (Dsh), ectopic Pros+ EEs appeared in renal tubes.
source: Consistently, MARCM clonal analysis revealed that, upon depletion of the Wnt/Wg pathway positive component Disheveled (Dsh), ectopic Pros+ EEs appeared in renal tubes (yellow arrowheads in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by MARCM clonal analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Wg signaling is essential for the MP-to-RP identity switch.
source: Therefore, Wg signaling is essential for the MP-to-RP identity switch.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing loss of renal identity upon Wg pathway inhibition.

claim: Upon overexpression of Wg ligand in all MPs, high levels of Cut expression were detected in all Esg+ progenitors dispersed throughout the midgut.
source: Upon overexpression of Wg ligand in all MPs, high levels of Cut expression were detected in all Esg+ progenitors dispersed throughout the midgut (arrowheads in Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Upon Wg overexpression, elevated number of Cut+ progenitors migrated onto renal tubules.
source: As a consequence, elevated number of Cut+ progenitors migrated onto renal tubules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Activation of Wg signaling in all MPs through overexpression of Arm-S10 exhibited similar effects as Wg overexpression.
source: In accordance, activation of Wg signaling in all MPs through overexpression of a constitutively-active form of the Wnt pathway effector β-catenin/Armadillo (Arm-S10) (Pai et al., 1997) exhibited similar effects as Wg overexpression (arrowheads in Figure 4J)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4J and citation to Pai et al., 1997.

claim: All MPs are competent to respond to Wg signaling.
source: demonstrating that all MPs are competent to respond to Wg signaling.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the Wg and Arm-S10 overexpression experiments showing ectopic Cut induction throughout the midgut.

claim: A steep Wg morphogen gradient provides a spatial cue to precisely select the pool of future RPs during metamorphosis.
source: Taken together, our data strongly support the notion that a steep Wg morphogen gradient provides a spatial cue to precisely select the pool of future RPs during metamorphosis (Figure 4K).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing the spatial restriction and requirement of Wg signaling.

claim: Membrane-tethered Wg failed to induce Cut expression in future RPs.
source: While membrane-tethered Wg sufficed to control fly patterning and growth (Alexandre et al., 2014), it failed to induce Cut expression in future RPs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and citation to Alexandre et al., 2014.

claim: The spread of Wg is necessary for activating Wg signaling in future RPs.
source: indicating that the spread of Wg is necessary for activating Wg signaling in these progenitors.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the membrane-tethered Wg experiment.

claim: The expression levels of wg-Gal4, wg-lacZ or Wg signaling reporter Fz3-GFP at the midgut-hindgut boundary remained relatively constant from second instar larval to early pupal stages.
source: Since the expression levels of wg-Gal4, wg-lacZ or Wg signaling reporter Fz3-GFP at the midgut-hindgut boundary remained relatively constant from second instar larval to early pupal stages (Figure 4A–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D), temporal cue(s) other than Wg ligand triggers Cut expression in future RPs at the onset of metamorphosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 4A-F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: The induction of Cut coincided with the pulse of the steroid hormone ecdysone released from the ring glands.
source: The induction of Cut coincided with the pulse of the steroid hormone ecdysone released from the ring glands (Ou and King-Jones, 2013; Yamanaka et al., 2013)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ou and King-Jones, 2013 and Yamanaka et al., 2013.

claim: Cut induction was abolished upon Esg+ progenitor-specific expression of EcR-DN.
source: Indeed, Cut induction was abolished upon Esg+ progenitor-specific expression of a dominant-negative form of the Ecdysone receptor (EcR-DN) (Brown et al., 2006) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citation to Brown et al., 2006.

claim: EcR was widely expressed in all cell types in the midgut at different developmental stages.
source: Since EcR was widely expressed in all cell types in the midgut at different developmental stages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Esg+ progenitor-specific depletion of the Broad complex (Br-C) phenocopied the effects of EcR-DN.
source: Supporting this notion, Esg+ progenitor-specific depletion of the Broad complex (Br-C) (Figure 5A), a crucial early response gene of the ecdysone signaling (Fletcher and Thummel, 1995; Karim et al., 1993), phenocopied the effects of EcR-DN.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and citations to Fletcher and Thummel, 1995 and Karim et al., 1993.

claim: Cut expression was normally turned on in future RPs upon downregulation of E74 and E75.
source: In comparison, Cut expression was normally turned on in future RPs upon downregulation of E74 and E75, the other two well-characterized ecdysone early response genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The steroid hormone ecdysone executes its control on Esg+ progenitor identity through specific downstream effector Br-C.
source: These observations indicated that the steroid hormone ecdysone executed its control on Esg+ progenitor identity through specific downstream effector Br-C.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the specific requirement for Br-C but not E74 or E75.

claim: Br-C protein expression was barely detectable in early third instar larvae.
source: Br-C protein expression was barely detectable in early third instar larvae, progressively increased starting mid third instar larval stage and peaked at the onset of metamorphosis, followed by a gradual decline (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal expression analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: Br-C protein expression progressively increased starting mid third instar larval stage and peaked at the onset of metamorphosis, followed by a gradual decline.
source: Br-C protein expression was barely detectable in early third instar larvae, progressively increased starting mid third instar larval stage and peaked at the onset of metamorphosis, followed by a gradual decline (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal expression analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-H.

claim: An ecdysone-EcR-Br regulatory axis induces Cut expression and dictates progenitor identity switch with temporal precision.
source: Together, our results revealed an ecdysone-EcR-Br regulatory axis, which induces Cut expression and dictates progenitor identity switch with temporal precision.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experiments showing the requirement for ecdysone signaling and Br-C.

claim: Depletion of Br-C abolished ectopic Cut expression induced by Wg or Arm-S10 overexpression in MPs.
source: Depletion of Br-C abolished ectopic Cut expression induced by Wg or Arm-S10 overexpression in MPs (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I)
evidence: The claim is supported by epistasis experiments shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Br-C acts downstream of or in parallel with the Wg pathway transcription activation complex TCF/Arm in cut induction.
source: demonstrating that Br-C acts downstream of or in parallel with the Wg pathway transcription activation complex TCF/Arm in cut induction.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the epistasis experiments.

claim: Wg pathway activity remained unaltered upon downregulation of ecdysone signaling.
source: Furthermore, Wg pathway activity, as indicated by the Fz3-GFP reporter, was highly responsive to a reduction in Wg signaling, but remained unaltered upon downregulation of ecdysone signaling (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter expression data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Wg and ecdysone signaling converge on the control of cut expression in a gene-specific manner.
source: Therefore, it is likely that Wg and ecdysone signaling converge on the control of cut expression in a gene-specific manner (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the epistasis experiments showing no general effect on Wg signaling by ecdysone pathway.

claim: Arm could be specifically coimmunoprecipitated with Br-C isoforms from HEK293T cell extracts.
source: Indeed, we found that Arm could be specifically coimmunoprecipitated with Br-C isoforms from HEK293T cell extracts and exhibited relatively strong binding affinity to Br-TNT-Z1, Br-Z2 and Br-Z4 (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Arm exhibited relatively strong binding affinity to Br-TNT-Z1, Br-Z2 and Br-Z4.
source: Indeed, we found that Arm could be specifically coimmunoprecipitated with Br-C isoforms from HEK293T cell extracts and exhibited relatively strong binding affinity to Br-TNT-Z1, Br-Z2 and Br-Z4 (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Overexpression of Br-Z1, Br-Z2 or TCF alone was barely able to precociously induce cut transcription at 9 hr BPF.
source: While overexpression of Br-Z1, Br-Z2 or TCF alone was barely able to precociously induce cut transcription at 9 hr before puparium formation (BPF) (induction rate of 0, 36 and 0% respectively; n = 11–12; arrowheads in Figure 6C)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from premature induction experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Coexpression of Br-Z1 or Br-Z2 with TCF dramatically enhanced Br activity in premature induction of cut expression.
source: coexpression of Br-Z1 or Br-Z2 with TCF dramatically enhanced Br activity in premature induction of cut expression (induction rate of 70 and 100% respectively; n = 9–17; arrowheads in Figure 6C)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from premature induction experiments shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Simultaneous overexpression of TCF and either Br-Z3 or Br-Z4 failed to induce premature cut expression.
source: Simultaneous overexpression of TCF and either Br-Z3 or Br-Z4 failed to induce premature cut expression, highlighting the importance of the isoform-specific C-terminal domain for Br functionality.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing lack of premature induction with these isoforms.

claim: Br-Z2 exhibited prominent and specific expression in Esg+ progenitors at 0 hr APF.
source: While Br-Z2, as stained by our newly-raised antibody (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), exhibited prominent and specific expression in Esg+ progenitors at 0 hr APF, Br-Z1 was undetectable in the midgut region (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Br-Z1 was undetectable in the midgut region at 0 hr APF.
source: While Br-Z2, as stained by our newly-raised antibody (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), exhibited prominent and specific expression in Esg+ progenitors at 0 hr APF, Br-Z1 was undetectable in the midgut region (Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The temporal expression pattern of Br-Z2 in Esg+ progenitors fully recapitulated that of Br-C.
source: Significantly, the temporal expression pattern of Br-Z2 in Esg+ progenitors fully recapitulated that of Br-C (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal expression analysis shown in Figure 6E.
